A2 opens with the gentlest possible step: to say something belongs to a person, put the name first and add -s — Annas Buch, Rohans Tasche, Frau Webers Büro. No apostrophe (unlike English), no article, no new endings. You already know das Buch von Anna from A1 — both are correct, but Annas Buch is shorter and sounds more natural, especially in writing. Names ending in s, ß, x, z take only an apostrophe: Max’ Handy, Felix’ Fahrrad, Hans’ Auto.

A2 opens with the smallest possible step. To show that something belongs to a person, you put the name first and add -s. Nothing else changes — no new endings, no article.
Name + s, written together, no apostrophe, no article.
German once had a full genitive ending on every noun. It survives intact only with names, which is why this is the one genitive form you can use everywhere without learning a table.
Frau Weber + s → Frau Webers Büro (-s on the LAST word)
Hindi "Anna ki kitaab" ka order same hai — naam pehle, cheez baad mein. Sirf -s naya hai, aur apostrophe kabhi nahi.
Annas Buch — name, then -s, then the thing.
No apostrophe (that is English) and no article.
Titles and full names: the -s goes on the last word.
To say something belongs to a person, put the name first and add -s — written together, no apostrophe. The owned thing follows, with no article before the name.

Unlike English, German writes the s without an apostrophe: Annas Buch, not Anna’s Buch. And no article before the name: Annas Buch, never die Annas Buch. With titles and full names the -s goes on the last word: Frau Webers Büro.

Hindi ke "Anna ki kitaab" jaisa hi hai — bas order ulta: naam pehle, phir -s, phir cheez: Annas Buch. English jaisa apostrophe nahi lagta: "Anna’s Buch" galat. Naam se pehle article bhi nahi: "die Annas Buch" galat.
Names ending in s, ß, x, z — apostrophe only
Name already ends in an s-sound? Write an apostrophe only — and add nothing to the pronunciation.
You cannot hear a second s after Max or Hans, so German does not write one. The apostrophe is there purely to mark on paper what the ear cannot catch.
Max → Max’ Handy (not Maxs, not Max’s)
Chaar akshar yaad rakho — s, ß, x, z. Inke baad sirf apostrophe, extra s nahi. Aur bolne mein koi farak nahi padta.
After s, ß, x, z: apostrophe only.
The pronunciation is unchanged — Max’ Handy sounds like "Max Handy".
Because you cannot hear it, speech often prefers das Handy von Max.
If the name already ends in an s-sound (s, ß, x, z), you cannot hear an extra -s — so German writes just an apostrophe and adds nothing to the pronunciation.

Pronunciation does not change: Max’ Handy sounds exactly like "Max Handy". Because you can’t hear the difference, spoken German often prefers das Handy von Max — both are correct. Never write an extra s: Maxs Handy, Max’s Handy.
Agar naam s, ß, x ya z par khatam hota hai, toh sirf apostrophe: Max’ Handy, Hans’ Auto. Bolne mein koi farak nahi — isliye bolchal mein log aksar das Handy von Max kehte hain. Dono sahi hain.
Annas Auto vs. das Auto von Anna
Both are correct. Name + s for writing, von + Dativ is very common in speech.
Likhna ho to Annas Auto (chhota, natural). Bolna ho to dono chalte hain — aur Hans, Max jaise naamon ke baad von zyada saaf hai, kyunki wahan -s sunai nahi deta.
Annas Auto = das Auto von Anna.
Prefer Name + s in writing; both are fine in speech.
You already know von + Dativ from A1. Both forms are correct — the difference is register and rhythm.

Rule of thumb: in writing, prefer Annas Auto — it is shorter and sounds more fluent. In speech, both are natural; after s/ß/x/z names, von is often clearer (das Auto von Hans). Never combine them: das Annas Auto von.

Dono sahi hain: Annas Auto = das Auto von Anna. Likhne mein Name + s zyada natural aur chhota hai. Bolne mein von bhi bilkul aam hai — khaas kar Hans, Max jaise naamon ke baad, jahan -s sunai nahi deta.
The owned noun keeps its own case
The -s marks the owner. The owned thing still takes whatever case the sentence gives it.
Wir fahren mit Papas Auto. → dative (after mit)
Name + s ek block hai jo saath-saath chalta hai — aur block ke andar article kabhi nahi aata: mit Papas Auto, "mit dem Papas Auto" nahi.
The Name + s block travels together.
The owned noun keeps its normal case.
The name takes the -s; the thing that is owned still plays its normal role in the sentence — nominative, accusative or dative. The Name + s block simply travels together.
Annas Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
Das Foto hängt in Frau Webers Büro.
Notice there is no article in the block: "mit Papas Auto", not mit dem Papas Auto. Everything you learned about Akkusativ and Dativ in A1 still applies around it.
Naam pe -s lagta hai, lekin cheez apna normal case rakhti hai: "Ich sehe Rohans Tasche" (Akkusativ), "mit Papas Auto" (Dativ). Block ke andar article nahi aata.
Now that you can say whose something is, you need the question that asks it. Wessen? = "whose?" — and it is the question word that goes with everything in this chapter.
It behaves like any other W-word: it takes slot 1, the verb follows in slot 2. What is new is that wessen comes directly before the noun, with no article — exactly like Name + s.
Wessen + noun (no article) + verb. Answer it with Name + s.
Wessen Handy ist das? → Das ist Annas Handy.
Wessen Schlüssel sind das? → Das sind Annas Schlüssel.

In everyday speech Germans very often avoid wessen and ask Wem gehört das? ("who does this belong to?") instead — with gehören + Dativ, which you already know from A1. Both are correct; wessen is the more written, more precise form, and it is what you will see in exercises.

Ab jab tum bata sakte ho ki cheez kiski hai, to poochhne ka tarika bhi aana chahiye. Wessen? ka matlab hai “kiska” ya “kiski”, aur yeh baaki W-words jaise hi chalta hai — pehli seat par wessen, aur doosri seat par verb. Naya sirf itna hai ki wessen ke baad seedha noun aata hai, article nahi — bilkul Name + s jaisa hi. Jawaab tum Name + s se dete ho: Wessen Handy ist das? — Das ist Annas Handy. Bolchal mein log aksar Wem gehört das? keh dete hain, jo gehören + Dativ hai aur A1 se tumhe aata hai. Woh bhi sahi hai, par likhne mein aur exercises mein wessen hi aata hai.
wessen ke baad article nahi lagta — jaise Name + s ke baad nahi lagta. Sawaal aur jawaab dono article-free hain.
Wessen + noun, no article, verb in slot 2.
Answer with Name + s: Das ist Annas Handy.
Plural thing → sind: Das sind Annas Schlüssel.
Spoken alternative: Wem gehört das? + dative.
You met the W-word slot in A1 (W-Fragen) and gehören + Dativ in Verben mit Dativ. Wessen simply fills that same slot 1, and Wem gehört …? reuses the dative verb you already have.
Four Name + s traps to avoid.
German writes Name + s together, without an apostrophe — unlike English.
Names ending in s, ß, x, z take an apostrophe only, no extra s.
No article before the possessive name.
The name comes first, then the thing — like Hindi "Anna ki kitaab".

Char galtiyan aksar hoti hain. Pehli, English wala apostrophe lagana — sahi hai Annas Buch, na ki “Anna’s Buch”. Doosri, jo naam s, ß, x ya z par khatam hote hain unme sirf apostrophe aata hai: Max’ Handy. Teesri, naam se pehle article lagana — “die Annas Buch” galat hai. Aur chauthi, order ulta kar dena — naam pehle aata hai aur cheez baad mein, bilkul jaise Hindi mein “Anna ki kitaab”.

Name + s inside a dative phrase — no article (this chapter).
Spätestens im August ist alles fertig.

Show possession by adding -s to a name (no apostrophe). Names ending in -s, -ß, -x, -z take an apostrophe only.
Name + s sounds more natural than "von + Name" in everyday speech. The apostrophe form (Max’) is only for names already ending in an s-sound.
Naam ke baad -s lagao (bina apostrophe): Annas Buch. Jo naam -s/-ß/-x/-z par khatam ho, sirf apostrophe: Max’ Handy.
The spoken past: haben or sein (position 2) + Partizip II (at the end). Movement/change verbs take sein.
Partizip II goes to the very end. Regular: ge-…-t (gemacht); many strong verbs: ge-…-en (gefahren, gekommen).
Perfekt = haben/sein (position 2) + Partizip II (sentence ke end mein). Chalne/badalne wale verbs sein lete hain: ich bin gefahren.
der/die/das and ein/eine change by case. Quick reminder of Nominativ vs. Akkusativ vs. Dativ (masculine is the mover).
Only the masculine changes in the accusative (der → den). The dative changes for everyone — the base for the possessive endings in Ch.7.
Akkusativ mein sirf masculine badalta hai (der→den). Dativ mein sab badalte hain (dem/der/dem/den) — yahi Ch.7 possessive endings ka base hai.
Ch.4 & 5 — weil / dass: verb to the end
Both weil (reason) and dass (reported thought/fact) open a Nebensatz — the conjugated verb goes to the end, with a comma before.
Ich lerne, weil ich bestehen will.

a2-11-wenn: One little word covers three everyday jobs: a condition (if), a repeated action (whenever) and a future plan (when). You already send the verb to the end after weil and dass. wenn works exactly the same way — and it does three everyday jobs at once. As a condition it means if: Wenn ich Zeit habe, lerne ich Deutsch. For a repeated action it means whenever: Immer wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause. For a future event it means when (with the present tense): Ich rufe dich an, wenn ich ankomme. In every case the conjugated verb goes to the end of the wenn-clause. And if you put the wenn-clause first, the main clause flips its verb to the front — verb, comma, verb: Wenn ich frei habe, gehe ich spazieren.

a2-12-reflexive-verben: Some German verbs point the action back at the doer, and they need a little mirror-word: the reflexive pronoun. Ich freue mich. Ich wäsche mich. A reflexive verb sends its action back to the doer, so it needs a little mirror-word — the reflexive pronoun. For most reflexive verbs the pronoun is accusative: ich → mich, du → dich, er/sie/es/sie/Sie → sich, wir → uns, ihr → euch. So: Ich freue mich. Ich wäsche mich. But the moment the sentence already has a direct object, the pronoun switches to the dative (mir, dir): Ich wäsche mir die Hände. Only ich and du change shape (mich/mir, dich/dir); everyone else keeps sich / uns / euch. Learn the little table once and a whole family of daily-life verbs — getting ready, feeling, meeting, relaxing — falls into place.

A reflexive verb needs a pronoun that mirrors the subject. Most reflexive verbs use the accusative pronoun; only ich and du have a separate dative form.

Nine prepositions are always followed by the dative — no thinking, no exceptions: aus, außer, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber. After any of them, the articles shift to their dative shapes: der/das → dem, die → der, and the plural adds an -n: mit den Freunden. Three combinations get squeezed into everyday contractions: zu dem → zum, zu der → zur, von dem → vom. Each preposition has a job — aus = origin, bei = at someone/somewhere, mit = transport/company, nach = to a city/country, zu = to a person/building, seit = since/for, von = from, gegenüber = opposite. Memorise the nine as a chant and the endings follow automatically.

Plural sabse dhokebaaz hai — article den aur noun par extra -n: mit den Freunden, mit den Kindern.
After a dative preposition the article changes shape. Masculine and neuter share dem; feminine is der; the plural is den and the noun gains an -n.
The plural is the sneaky one: article den and an extra -n on the noun (den Freunden, den Kindern) — unless the plural already ends in -n or -s. Indefinite: einem (m/n), einer (f).

Dativ mein articles aise badalte hain: masculine aur neuter dono dem lete hain, feminine der, aur plural den — saath hi plural noun par ek extra -n bhi lagta hai, jaise mit den Freunden. Indefinite article ki forms einem (m/n) aur einer (f) hain.
Use the contraction by default: zum, zur, vom, beim.
Feminine der se zur, masc/neut dem se zum. Rozmarra mein yahi bolte hain — "zu dem Arzt" ajeeb lagta hai.
Three preposition + article pairs are almost always squeezed together in speech and writing.
zum, zur, vom (and beim) are the everyday forms — use them. Writing "zu dem Arzt" isn’t wrong, but it sounds unnatural. Remember: zu der → zur (feminine), zu dem → zum (masc/neut).

Rozmarra German mein chaar contractions bahut common hain: zu dem se zum, zu der se zur, von dem se vom, aur bei dem se beim. Normally inhi ko bolna behtar hai, kyunki poora form jaise zu dem Arzt thoda ajeeb lagta hai.
Each dative preposition owns a job. Pick by meaning, then the dative follows automatically.
The famous pair to keep apart: nach for cities/countries/home (nach Berlin, nach Hause) vs zu for people and buildings (zum Arzt, zur Schule).

Har preposition ka apna kaam hai. aus origin batata hai, bei kisi ke paas hona, mit transport ya saath, nach sheher ya desh ki taraf jaana, zu kisi person ya building ki taraf, seit kab se, aur gegenüber saamne. Sabse zyada confusion nach aur zu mein hoti hai — sheher ke liye nach, aur person ya building ke liye zu.
Bus is masculine; dative singular → dem, not den.
zu + dem contracts to zum — don’t drop the article.
aus takes the dative; feminine die → der.
For a person/building use zu(m), not nach.

Char galtiyan common hain. mit dem Bus sahi hai, mit den Bus nahi. zum Bahnhof mein article chhodna nahi hai. Feminine noun ke saath Dativ der hota hai, jaise aus der Schule. Aur kisi person ya building ke liye zu ya zum use karo, nach nahi.
Two steps handle every dative-preposition sentence.
origin → aus · at → bei · transport → mit · city → nach · building/person → zu · since → seit · from → von · opposite → gegenüber
2. Put the noun in the dative
dem (m/n) · der (f) · den + -n (pl) — and contract: zum, zur, vom
The nine prepositions never change case — so once you’ve chosen one, you never have to ask "which case?". It’s always dative.

Do step mein socho. Pehle matlab dekh kar preposition chuno, phir uske baad wale noun ko Dativ mein daalo — dem, der ya den (+-n) — aur ho sake to contract kar do (zum, zur, vom). In nau prepositions ke saath case ka sawaal hi nahi uthta, kyunki yeh sab Dativ lete hain.
seit + Dativ for a period up to now (this chapter).
ein Jahr → einem Jahr after seit (this chapter).
bei + Dativ = at someone’s place (this chapter).
bei + Dativ; mein → meiner (recycled — Possessiv Dativ).
neben (this chapter, used with dative for location).
plural dative: die → den + noun -n (this chapter).
dieses Jahr → diesem Jahr after seit (this chapter).

The one test: Wohin? or Wo?

English uses two different words for this — "in" the kitchen vs "into" the kitchen. German keeps one preposition and lets the article carry the difference. So the case is doing the work "into" does in English.
Wohin? → Akk: Ich gehe in die Schule. (jaa rahe ho)
Wo? → Dat: Ich bin in der Schule. (wahaan ho)
Ek hi sawaal: hila raha hoon ya pehle se wahaan hoon? Hila raha hoon → Akkusativ. Wahaan hoon → Dativ. Preposition wahi rehta hai, sirf article badalta hai.

German pairs its “put” and “be” verbs. One verb of each pair is a direction verb (you’re moving something — Wohin? → Akkusativ), the other a position verb (it’s already there — Wo? → Dativ). Compare: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch (direction) vs. Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch (position). The five pairs: stellen/stehen, legen/liegen, setzen/sitzen, hängen/hängen, stecken/stecken. The direction verbs are regular (legen – legte – gelegt); the position verbs are often irregular (liegen – lag – gelegen). This is Chapter 14’s wohin/wo rule made into verbs — pick the verb, and the case comes with it.

The direction verbs take a direct object (I put something) — that’s why they trigger the accusative. The position verbs describe a state, so they go with the dative. hängen and stecken use the same word for both directions. hängen still separates them in the past (hängte/gehängt for the move, hing/gehangen for the position), but stecken has identical past forms — so with stecken only the case tells you which job it is.

A direct question stands alone: Wo wohnst du? Wrap it inside a polite frame — Kannst du mir sagen, …? or Ich weiß nicht, … — and it becomes an indirect question: Kannst du mir sagen, wo du wohnst? Two fixed rules, no exceptions: a W-word (wer, was, wann, wo, wohin, woher, warum, wie, wie viel, wie lange, welcher) opens the clause when the original question had one; ob opens it when the original was a plain yes/no question. Either way, the conjugated verb moves to the very end — exactly like weil, dass and wenn. There is no inversion after the question word: never wo wohnst du inside the frame, always wo du wohnst.

The moment you put the question inside a bigger sentence, it stops being a question of its own — it becomes a piece of the main sentence. German marks that with verb-final order, exactly as it does after weil, dass and wenn.

Wrap a direct question in a polite frame, and it becomes an indirect question. Two things change: the question word (or ob) starts a subordinate clause, and the verb slides to the end.

Common frames: Kannst du mir sagen, … / Ich weiß nicht, … / Weißt du, … / Er/Sie fragt, … / Ich frage mich, … / … möchte wissen, …. A comma always separates the frame from the indirect clause.

If the direct question had a W-word, that same word opens the indirect clause — and the verb still goes to the end.

ob = whether; wenn = if (condition). Different jobs.
If the direct question has no question word (a plain yes/no question), open the indirect clause with ob.

ob translates as "whether" or "if" — but never confuse it with wenn (if = condition, recycled from Ch.11). Here ob only introduces a reported yes/no question.
Agar direct sawaal mein koi question word nahi (sirf haan/na), toh ob se shuru karo. ob = whether/if, lekin wenn (condition) se alag hai.
The single biggest trap: after the question word or ob, do not invert the verb and subject. Send the conjugated verb to the very end, just like weil/dass/wenn.

Ich weiß nicht, wo du wohnst.
Kannst du sagen, ob kommt er?
Kannst du sagen, ob er kommt?
Ich frage, warum bist du müde?
Ich frage, warum du müde bist.
In the Perfekt or with a modal, the conjugated helper is truly last, after the participle/infinitive: …, ob sie den Vorschlag genehmigt hat.

Every Perfekt sentence is a bracket: the helper verb (haben or sein) sits in position 2, and the Partizip II waits at the very end. Everything else lives inside the bracket.

Partizip II shapes — regular, irregular, separable
Regular ge…t · irregular ge…en · separable puts ge in the middle · inseparable takes no ge.

You know all three patterns from A1. This chapter’s verbs cover every one:
Separable verbs tuck ge- inside: teilgenommen, ausgewählt, zugehört. Inseparable prefixes (be-, ver-, er-) take no ge- at all: beendet, verstanden.

Partizip ke teen shapes hain. Regular verbs ge-…-t lete hain, jaise gekauft aur gemietet. Irregular verbs ge-…-en lete hain, jaise geritten aur gegangen. Separable verbs mein ge- beech mein aa jaata hai: teilgenommen. Aur be- ya ver- wale verbs mein ge- bilkul nahi lagta: beendet, verstanden.
Time expressions that call the Perfekt
These words anchor a sentence in the past — hear one, expect the Perfekt frame around it:
schon and noch nicht are a pair — the question "Hast du schon …?" invites either "Ja, ich habe schon …" or "Nein, noch nicht."
Yeh time words sunte hi Perfekt ka frame taiyaar rakho. schon = "ho gaya", noch nicht = "abhi nahi hua". "Hast du schon gegessen?" → "Nein, noch nicht."
Questions and nicht in the Perfekt
Questions reuse the same bracket. W-questions put the question word first, helper second; Ja/Nein questions put the helper first. nicht stands right before the final Partizip.
Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?
Hast du den Kurs schon beendet?
The Partizip never moves — not for questions, not for negation. Only the front of the sentence changes.
Sawaal mein bhi bracket wahi rehta hai: "Was hast du gemacht?", "Hast du beendet?". nicht aksar Partizip ke theek pehle aata hai: "Ich habe das nicht verstanden."
Movement takes sein, not haben — gehen, fahren, reiten, folgen.

The core verbs and the pattern
With two nouns the usual order is person first, thing second: Dativ → Akkusativ.
Ich gebe meinem Freund (Dat.) ein Buch (Akk.).
↑ kaun paata hai ↑ kya milta hai
Do sawaal poochho: kisko? → Dativ. kya? → Akkusativ. English bhi wahi karti hai: "give him the book".
These verbs always take two objects: a Dativ object (who receives) and an Akkusativ object (what is received). The pattern never changes: Subjekt → Verb → Dativ → Akkusativ.
Ich gebe meinem Freund ein Buch.
Wir schicken unserer Mutter eine Nachricht.
Ask two questions for every one of these verbs: Who receives? → Dativ. What is received? → Akkusativ.

In verbs ke saath usually do cheezein aati hain: kisko? — yaani Dativ, aur kya? — yaani Akkusativ. Normal sentence mein aksar order hota hai: Subjekt → Verb → Dativ → Akkusativ. Aage dekhoge ki pronouns aane par yeh order badal jaata hai.
When both objects are nouns, the Dativ object (the person) comes before the Akkusativ object (the thing).
Ich gebe meinem Bruder das Geld.
Sie zeigt ihrem Lehrer die Hausaufgabe.
Wir schicken unserer Mutter eine Nachricht.
The receiver is always in the Dativ — never Nominativ or Akkusativ: meinem Bruder, not meinen Bruder.
Jab dono objects noun hote hain, to insaan pehle aata hai (Dativ) aur cheez baad mein (Akkusativ). In verbs ke saath jo cheez paata hai, woh Dativ mein hi rehta hai.
Both objects as pronouns? The order flips: Akkusativ before Dativ.
nouns: Ich gebe ihm das Buch.
pronouns: Ich gebe es ihm. ← Akk. first
German puts the shortest, most familiar information first. A pronoun is shorter than a noun, and es is the shortest of all — so it moves to the front of the pair.
Noun ke saath: insaan pehle. Dono pronoun: cheez pehle (es ihm). Aur ek noun + ek pronoun ho to pronoun usually pehle aata hai.
Mixed → the pronoun comes first, whatever its case.
Once both objects turn into pronouns, the order flips: the Akkusativ pronoun comes before the Dativ pronoun.
With a noun for the thing
Kannst du mir das Buch geben?
With one noun and one pronoun, the pronoun always comes first, regardless of case: Ich gebe ihm das Buch. / Ich gebe es meinem Freund.

Jab dono objects pronoun ban jaate hain, to order badal jaata hai — Akkusativ pronoun pehle aata hai aur Dativ pronoun baad mein. Aur agar ek noun aur ek pronoun ho, to pronoun aksar pehle aata hai, chahe uska case koi bhi ho.
Ich gebe meinen Freund ein Buch. → Ich gebe meinem Freund ein Buch. — the receiver must be Dativ (meinem), not Akkusativ (meinen).
Ich erkläre die Grammatik den Studenten. → Ich erkläre den Studenten die Grammatik. — with two nouns, Dativ (the person) comes first.
Ich schicke mein Vater eine Nachricht. → Ich schicke meinem Vater eine Nachricht. — Vater needs the Dativ ending on the possessive: meinem.
Ich gebe ihm ihn. → Ich gebe es ihm. — with two pronouns, Akkusativ comes before Dativ, and check the pronoun's gender (es for das Buch, not ihn).
Common galtiyaan: receiver Dativ mein hona chahiye; do noun ho toh Dativ pehle; possessive ko bhi Dativ ending do; do pronoun ho toh Akkusativ pehle aata hai.

It does four jobs — polite request (Könntest du…?), suggestion (Wir könnten…), possibility (Es könnte…), and hypothetical ability (Ich könnte…) — always softer and less direct than plain kann.

deshalb and trotzdem — result vs. contrast
Both connect two main clauses. deshalb (therefore) marks the expected result of the first clause. trotzdem (nevertheless) marks an unexpected contrast.
Ich bin krank. Deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
Es regnet. Trotzdem gehen wir spazieren.
Both are adverbs, not subordinating conjunctions — they connect two separate main clauses, each with its own full sentence structure.
deshalb = isliye (expected result). trotzdem = phir bhi (unexpected contrast). Dono do alag main clauses ko jodte hain.
deshalb and trotzdem occupy position one of their clause. Because the verb always stays in position two, it comes immediately after the connector — before the subject.
This is the same inversion pattern as any position-one adverb: connector → verb → subject → rest.
deshalb aur trotzdem clause ke position 1 par aate hain, isliye verb position 2 par aa jaata hai — matlab connector ke seedhe baad, subject se pehle.

weil and deshalb express the same cause-and-result idea, but from opposite directions and with different word order. weil opens a subordinate clause (verb at the end); deshalb opens a second main clause (verb in position two).
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten möchte.
Ich möchte in Deutschland arbeiten. Deshalb lerne ich Deutsch.
Ich bin krank, weil ich Fieber habe.
Ich habe Fieber. Deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
Never combine weil and deshalb in the same sentence — pick one direction and stick with it.

weil aur deshalb ek hi cause-result idea batate hain, par ulti direction se. weil ek subordinate clause banata hai jisme verb end mein jaata hai, aur deshalb ek naya main clause shuru karta hai jisme verb position 2 par rehta hai. Dono ko ek hi sentence mein saath nahi jodna.
Deshalb ich gehe. → Deshalb gehe ich. — the verb must come right after deshalb, before the subject.
Trotzdem ich bleibe. → Trotzdem bleibe ich. — same rule for trotzdem.
Ich bin müde, weil deshalb ich schlafe. → Ich bin müde. Deshalb schlafe ich. — never stack weil and deshalb together.
Trotzdem weil es regnet, gehen wir. → Es regnet. Trotzdem gehen wir. — trotzdem and weil don't combine into one connector.

Indirekte Frage — W-word or ob, verb to the end

The definite article (der/die/das, and its case forms den/dem/der/die/den) already shows gender and case. Because the article does that job, the adjective almost always just adds -e or -en — never any other ending.

Only two cells in the whole table use -e; everything else — Akkusativ masculine, all of Dativ, and the entire plural — uses -en.
-e appears in exactly three places: Nominativ (all three genders) and Akkusativ feminine/neuter. Everywhere else in this table is -en.
-e sirf kuch hi jagah aata hai: Nominativ mein teeno gender ke saath, aur Akkusativ mein feminine aur neuter ke saath. Baaki har jagah -en aata hai.
These are the only cells where the adjective keeps -e:
Yaad rakhne ka tarika yeh hai: -e Nominativ mein aur Akkusativ ke feminine/neuter mein rehta hai, aur uske baad har jagah -en aa jaata hai.
der kleinen Hund → der kleine Hund — Nominativ masculine takes -e, not -en.
den kleine Hund → den kleinen Hund — Akkusativ masculine takes -en, not -e.
dem kleine Mann → dem kleinen Mann — Dativ always takes -en.
die schönen Tasche → die schöne Tasche — a single feminine bag (Nom./Akk.) takes -e, not -en (that ending is for plural).

Char galtiyan common hain. Nominativ masculine mein -e aata hai, -en nahi. Akkusativ masculine mein -en aata hai, -e nahi. Dativ mein har gender ke saath -en aata hai. Aur feminine singular mein -e rehta hai — -en sirf plural mein aata hai.

Picture a timeline: a single dot in the past is als; anything repeated, or in the present/future, or a condition, is wenn. Both send the conjugated verb to the end of their own clause, and both trigger inversion in the following main clause.
Past one-time (a single dot on the timeline) → als. Present/Future/Habit (repeating or ongoing) → wenn.

Timeline socho. Agar baat past ke ek specific time ki hai to als aayega. Aur agar cheez baar-baar hoti hai, ya baat present, future ya condition ki hai, to wenn aayega. Dono ke baad verb clause ke end mein jaata hai, aur agar clause pehle aaye to main clause verb se shuru hoti hai.
Wenn ich klein war, spielte ich Fußball. → Als ich klein war, … — a specific past period uses als, not wenn.
Als ich Zeit habe, lese ich. → Wenn ich Zeit habe, … — a present habit uses wenn, not als.
Als es morgen regnet, … → Wenn es morgen regnet, … — the future always uses wenn.
Wenn ich gestern krank war, … → Als ich gestern krank war, … — a specific past day (gestern) is a one-time event, so als.

Char galtiyan common hain. Past ke specific period ke liye als chahiye, wenn nahi. Present mein jo cheez regularly hoti hai, uske liye wenn aata hai. Future ke liye bhi wenn hi aata hai. Aur agar koi specific din past mein hai, jaise gestern, to als use karo.

Complete: "___ ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause." (present habit)
A repeated present situation uses wenn.
Which connector is used for the future?
wenn covers future situations — als is never used for the future.
Als es morgen regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.
Wenn es morgen regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.
Ob es morgen regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.
Wenn ich gestern krank war, blieb ich zu Hause.
Als ich gestern krank war, blieb ich zu Hause.
Ob ich gestern krank war, blieb ich zu Hause.
A specific past day (gestern) is a one-time event, so als is correct.
als is used only for a single, completed event in the past — never for repeated actions, the present, or the future.
wenn covers everything else: repeated actions, the present, the future, and conditions.
Both send the verb to the end of their own clause, and both trigger inversion in the following main clause: Als ich klein war, wohnte ich in Delhi.
Did it happen only once, in the past? → als. Everything else (repeated, present, future, condition)? → wenn.
A specific past day or moment (gestern, letzte Woche, als ich ankam) is still a one-time event — use als, not wenn.
The future never uses als — always wenn, even for a single planned future event.

jemand = someone, an unspecified person. niemand = no one, no person at all. Both are singular, third-person; the Akkusativ can add -en, and the Dativ adds -em (review only this chapter).
jemand ka matlab hai “koi”, jab tum nahi jaante ki kaun. niemand ka matlab hai “koi nahi”. Akkusativ mein in dono par -en lag sakta hai: jemanden, niemanden.
etwas = something (unspecified). nichts = nothing. alles = everything, as a whole. None of the three change form for case.
etwas Neues, etwas Gutes — after etwas/nichts, an adjective is capitalised and takes -es, like a noun.
etwas ka matlab hai “kuch”, nichts ka “kuch nahi”, aur alles ka “sab kuch”. In teeno ki form case ke hisaab se nahi badalti, isliye yeh aasaan hain.
jeder treats every member of a group individually — it takes a singular verb, like a "der-word". alle treats the group as a whole — it takes a plural verb.
jeder ka matlab hai har koi, ek-ek karke — isliye iske saath singular verb aata hai. alle ka matlab hai sab log ek group ki tarah — isliye iske saath plural verb aata hai.
These four describe an unspecified quantity of people or things — all take plural nouns and plural verbs.
manche ka matlab hai kuch log, ek hisse ki tarah. viele ka matlab bahut se, einige ka thode se, aur wenige ka bahut kam — jisme kami par zor hota hai.
Alles klar. — All clear / got it. Alles Gute. — All the best. Nichts passiert. — No harm done. Etwas Neues. — Something new.
Jeder sind … → Jeder ist … — jeder always takes a singular verb.
Alle ist … → Alle sind … — alle always takes a plural verb.
Ich sehe niemand. → Ich sehe niemanden. — as a direct object, niemand takes the Akkusativ -en ending.
Ich habe nichts nicht. → Ich habe nichts. — never double the negation.

der / die / das — the definite article, at a glance
Learn the noun with its article. And every plural is die.
Plural mein gender khatam — sab die. Yeh sabse sasta jeet hai.
Every German noun carries a gender — masculine, feminine or neuter — and the definite article (English the) shows it. In the plural, all three collapse into one: always die.
der Rentner, der Platz, der Eingang
die Gärtnerin, die Arbeit, die Meinung
das Land, das Fach, das Berufsleben
die Plätze, die Fächer, die Meinungen
The plural is the easy one: die for everything — die Rentner, die Gärtnerinnen, die Länder. Always learn a noun with its article, never alone: not "Platz" but "der Platz".

Har German noun ka ek gender hota hai: der (m), die (f), das (n). Plural mein hamesha die. Noun hamesha article ke saath yaad karo — "Platz" nahi, "der Platz". Hindi mein gender natural aata hai; German mein yaad karna padta hai.
The indefinite article (English a/an) has just two nominative shapes: ein for masculine and neuter, eine for feminine. There is no plural — "a books" makes no sense in German either.
Note that masculine and neuter share ein in the nominative — the difference only shows up in the accusative and dative (next card). Its negative, kein/keine, behaves exactly the same way.
Indefinite article ki do hi shapes hain: ein masculine aur neuter ke liye, aur eine feminine ke liye. Plural mein indefinite article hota hi nahi. kein/keine bhi bilkul isi tarah chalte hain.
Across the cases — only the masculine really changes
In the accusative only masculine moves (der→den, ein→einen). In the dative everything moves.
Akk: den / die / das / die ← only masc. changed
Akkusativ mein sirf masculine par nazar rakho. Dativ mein har jagah m ya r sunai deta hai: dem, der, dem, den.
Dative: dem / der / dem / den, and the plural noun adds -n.
Feminine and neuter never change in the accusative.
You met this in A1. The comforting news for review: in the accusative, only the masculine changes. Feminine, neuter and plural look identical to the nominative.
Watch the masculine journey: der Mann → ich sehe den Mann → mit dem Mann, and ein → einen → einem. In the dative plural the noun itself gains an -n: mit den Kindern.
Achhi khabar: Akkusativ mein sirf masculine badalta hai (der→den, ein→einen). fem/neut/plural same rehte hain. Dativ mein sab badalte hain: dem/der/dem, aur plural noun par extra -n: mit den Kindern.
Endings are good guesses: -in -ung -heit -keit -schaft → die · -er -ling -ismus → der · -chen -lein -um -ment → das.
Ending dekh kar andaaza lagao — aur -chen/-lein to hamesha das hota hai, chahe matlab kuch bhi ho (das Mädchen).
Gender feels random, but noun endings predict it surprisingly often. These three groups are reliable enough to lean on:
die Gärtnerin, die Schülerin, die Behinderung, die Meinung
der Rentner, der Arzthelfer, der Altenpfleger
die Schul·uniform (die Uniform), der Vokabel·test (der Test)
For a compound, only the last noun decides: der Beruf + das Leben = das Berufsleben; die Schule + der Abschluss = der Schulabschluss. That one rule settles most of this chapter’s long words.

Ending dekh kar gender ka andaaza lag jaata hai. -in, -ung aur -heit wale nouns aksar die lete hain; -er aur -ling wale der; aur -chen aur -um wale das. Compound word mein sirf aakhri hissa gender decide karta hai, isliye das Berufsleben (kyunki das Leben) aur der Schulabschluss (kyunki der Abschluss).
definite vs indefinite — which one, when?
Same choice as English the vs a: use the indefinite when something is new or non-specific, and the definite once it’s known or unique.
One handy exception: after sein/werden, professions take no article — "Er ist Altenpfleger", "Sie wird Gärtnerin". Just like we’d say it in Hindi.

These common verbs always pair with an Akkusativ preposition. The preposition never changes, no matter what the verb means elsewhere.
Worauf wartest du? → Auf den Bus.
Ich erinnere mich an die Stimme.
Woran erinnerst du dich? → An die Stimme.
Ich freue mich auf das Festival.
Worauf freust du dich? → Auf das Festival.
Woran glaubst du? → An einen Neuanfang.
Wofür interessierst du dich? → Für Pop.
Ich entscheide mich für den Schritt.
Wofür entscheidest du dich? → Für den Schritt.
Ich kümmere mich um die Überweisung.
Worum kümmerst du dich? → Um die Überweisung.

When the object of a fixed verb-preposition pair is a thing, you don't ask "was" — you fuse wo(r)- onto the preposition, written as ONE word. The answer fuses da(r)- the same way.

Before a vowel, wo/da add an -r-: wo + auf = worauf, da + an = daran (an starts with a vowel, so technically no -r- is added here — but wo + an = woran also needs the -r- for pronunciation ease). Learn each pair as a fixed chunk.
Jab object koi cheez ho, to was se sawaal nahi banta. Preposition ke saath wo(r)- jod do, aur poora ek shabd bana do. Jawaab mein usi preposition ke saath da(r)- aata hai.
People: the preposition stays, wem/wen replaces them
When the object is a person, never use wo(r)-/da(r)-. Keep the plain preposition and add wem (Dativ) or wen (Akkusativ).
❌ Womit sprichst du? is wrong when the object is a person — always Mit wem?
Jab object koi insaan ho, to wo(r)- aur da(r)- use nahi hote. Preposition wahi rehti hai, aur uske baad wem (Dativ) ya wen (Akkusativ) aata hai.

Wo auf wartest du? → Worauf wartest du? — wo(r)+Präposition is always ONE word, never split.
Ich warte da auf. → Ich warte darauf. — da(r)+Präposition is always ONE word too.
Mit was sprichst du? → Womit sprichst du? (for things) / Mit wem sprichst du? (for people).
Worauf sprichst du? → Worüber sprichst du? — sprechen pairs with über (about a topic), not auf.
Woran wartest du? → Worauf wartest du? — warten always pairs with auf, never an.
Do galtiyan common hain. wo(r)- aur da(r)- ek hi shabd mein likhe jaate hain, unhe todna nahi hai. Aur kisi insaan ke liye womit ya wofür nahi aata — wahan preposition ke saath wem ya wen aata hai.

Konjunktiv II makes German softer and more polite. ich habe → ich hätte (I would have / I'd like). ich bin → ich wäre (I would be). ich will → ich würde gern + Infinitiv (I would like to). Use them for wishes (Ich hätte gern…), polite requests (Könnten Sie…? Würden Sie…?), offers (Ich würde Ihnen gern helfen), preferences (Ich würde lieber…), and friendly advice (An deiner Stelle würde ich…).

Konjunktiv II makes a sentence softer, more polite, or hypothetical. Three verbs change the most often at A2.
I would have / I'd like (a thing)
I would be (a state, a place)

Konjunktiv II sentence ko polite ya hypothetical bana deta hai. habe se hätte banta hai (jab koi cheez chahiye), bin se wäre (jab kahin hona ho), aur will ki jagah würde gern + Infinitiv aata hai (jab kuch karna ho).
Use hätte gern for wanting a thing, wäre gern for wanting to be somewhere or in a state, and würde gern + Infinitiv for wanting to do an action.
Faisla aise karo: koi cheez chahiye to hätte gern, kahin hona ya kisi state mein hona ho to wäre gern, aur kuch karna ho to würde gern ke saath Infinitiv.
Formal requests use the Sie-form of könnte, würde, or hätte. Offers use ich könnte or ich würde gern.
Formal request ke liye Könnten Sie …?, Würden Sie …? ya Hätten Sie …? use karo. Aur kuch offer karna ho to ich könnte ya ich würde gern theek rehta hai.
würde lieber / hätte lieber express a preference. An deiner Stelle würde ich… gives friendly advice by imagining yourself in someone else's position.
Ich würde lieber zu Hause bleiben.
An deiner Stelle würde ich mehr lernen.
This chapter does not cover the unreal past (ich wäre lieber früher gekommen) beyond simple recognition — it is not tested.

Preference batane ke liye würde lieber ya hätte lieber aata hai. Aur advice dene ke liye an deiner Stelle würde ich … bahut natural lagta hai — matlab khud ko saamne wale ki jagah rakh kar baat karna.
Ich würde gern bin in Deutschland. → Ich wäre gern in Deutschland. — würde needs an Infinitiv at the end, not a conjugated verb like "bin".
Ich hätte gehen. → Ich würde gern gehen. — for an action, use würde + Infinitiv, not hätte + Infinitiv.
Würdest Sie mir helfen? → Würden Sie mir helfen? — the formal Sie-form is always würden, never würdest.
Ich wäre einen Kaffee. → Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee. — wäre is for being/state, not for having a thing.

Teen galtiyan common hain. würde ke baad Infinitiv aata hai, koi conjugated form nahi. Kaam ke liye würde, cheez ke liye hätte, aur state ke liye wäre use karo. Aur polite Sie ke saath würden aata hai, würdest nahi.

A relative clause (Relativsatz) describes a noun with a whole extra sentence, joined by der, die, das, or plural die. In this chapter, the relative pronoun is always the SUBJECT of its clause — so it matches the gender/number of the noun it describes, and the verb moves to the end. Das ist der Mann, der hier arbeitet.

A relative clause (Relativsatz) adds information about a noun (the Bezugswort/antecedent) using a Relativpronomen. When the pronoun is the SUBJECT of its own clause, use these Nominativ forms — they match the gender/number of the antecedent noun, not the verb that follows.

Relativsatz kisi noun ke baare mein extra jaankari deta hai. Jab relative pronoun us clause ka subject hota hai, to uska gender aur number us noun se match karta hai jiske baare mein baat ho rahi hai: masculine ke liye der, feminine ke liye die, neuter ke liye das, aur plural ke liye die.
Combine two short sentences into one fluent sentence: the second sentence's subject becomes the relative pronoun, and its verb moves to the end.

Do chhote sentences milkar ek fluent sentence ban jaate hain. Doosre sentence ka subject relative pronoun ban jaata hai, aur uska verb clause ke end mein chala jaata hai.
Word order: verb goes to the end
A relative clause is a Nebensatz (subordinate clause): main clause → comma → relative pronoun → rest of the clause → conjugated verb at the very end.
Ich kenne den Lehrer, der in Berlin wohnt.
Das ist die Tasche, die sehr teuer ist.
Wir besuchen die Freunde, die aus Indien kommen.

Relativsatz bhi ek Nebensatz hai, isliye structure jaana-pehchana hai: pehle main clause, phir comma, phir relative pronoun, phir baaki clause, aur end mein conjugated verb — bilkul jaise weil, dass aur wenn ke saath hota hai.
der Mann der arbeitet hier → der Mann, der hier arbeitet — always put a comma before the relative pronoun.
Das ist die Frau, die spricht Deutsch. → Das ist die Frau, die Deutsch spricht. — the verb must go to the end of the clause.
Das ist das Auto, der neu ist. → Das ist das Auto, das neu ist. — das Auto is neuter, so use das, not der.
Das sind Studenten, der Deutsch lernen. → Das sind Studenten, die Deutsch lernen. — plural nouns always take die.
Teen galtiyan common hain: comma bhool jaana, verb ko end mein na bhejna, aur pronoun ka gender us noun se match na karna jiske baare mein baat ho rahi hai.

From Nominativ to Akkusativ: only der changes
When the relative pronoun is the direct OBJECT of its clause (not the subject), use the Akkusativ form. Only the masculine changes — feminine, neuter, and plural stay identical to Nominativ.

Jab relative pronoun us clause ka direct object hota hai, subject nahi, to Akkusativ form aati hai. Achhi baat yeh hai ki sirf masculine badalta hai — der se den. Feminine, neuter aur plural Nominativ jaise hi rehte hain.
Subject or object? A quick test

Ask: is there already another subject inside the relative clause? If yes, the relative pronoun is the object (Akkusativ). If the relative pronoun itself is doing the action, it's the subject (Nominativ).
der Mann, der hier arbeitet — der does the working
der Film, den ich gesehen habe — ich does the seeing, den is what's seen

Test simple hai: dekho ki clause mein pehle se koi aur subject hai ya nahi. Agar hai, to relative pronoun object hai aur Akkusativ aayega. Aur agar pronoun khud kaam kar raha hai, to woh subject hai aur Nominativ aayega.
The Akkusativ relative pronoun always matches the antecedent noun's gender/number, and the verb goes to the end.
Das ist der Film, den ich gesehen habe.
Das ist die Sendung, die ich höre.
Das ist das Buch, das ich lese.
Das sind die Songs, die ich mag.
Akkusativ relative pronoun bhi us noun ke gender aur number se match karta hai jiske baare mein baat ho rahi hai, aur verb clause ke end mein jaata hai.
Das ist der Film, der ich gesehen habe. → Das ist der Film, den ich gesehen habe. — der Film is the object here (ich is the subject), so it needs den.
Ich kenne die Frau, die er liebt sie. → Ich kenne die Frau, die er liebt. — never repeat the object with a second pronoun (sie) after the relative pronoun.
Das ist das Buch, das ich es lese. → Das ist das Buch, das ich lese. — same mistake: no extra pronoun (es) is needed.
Do galtiyan common hain: masculine object ke liye den bhool jaana, aur relative pronoun ke baad ek aur pronoun jaise sie ya es dobara lagana — uski zaroorat nahi hoti.
Is the relative pronoun the OBJECT of its clause (someone else is doing the action)? → Use Akkusativ. Then check gender: masculine → den, feminine → die, neuter → das, plural → die.
Pehle dekho ki relative pronoun object hai — matlab kaam koi aur kar raha hai. Agar haan, to Akkusativ aayega. Uske baad gender check karo: masculine den, feminine die, neuter das, plural die.
die — Akkusativ relative pronoun, feminine, same as Nominativ (this chapter).
den — Akkusativ relative pronoun, masculine. This is the ONLY form that changes from Nominativ der (this chapter).

After der/die/das, adjectives take -e in the Nominativ singular and -en almost everywhere else. After ein-words (ein, mein, dein…), the article itself sometimes carries no ending, so the adjective steps in: masculine Nom. sg. -er, neuter Nom./Akk. sg. -es.
der/die/das ke baad adjective -e leta hai (Nominativ singular mein) ya -en. Aur ein-word ke baad masculine Nominativ mein -er aata hai aur neuter mein -es.
als describes ONE single event in the past. wenn describes a repeated/habitual past event, or any present/future condition.
Als ich meine erste Prüfung machte, war ich nervös.
Wenn man gut vorbereitet ist, ist man ruhiger.
als past ke ek specific time ke liye aata hai, aur wenn baar-baar hone wali situation ke liye, ya present aur future ki condition ke liye.
jemand/niemand (people), etwas/nichts (things), alles/jeder/alle/manche/viele/einige/wenige (quantities) — none of them take an article.

Indefinitpronomen teen groups mein baant lo: logon ke liye jemand aur niemand, cheezon ke liye etwas aur nichts, aur quantity ke liye alles, jeder, alle, manche, viele. In sab ke saath article nahi lagta.
Fixed-preposition verbs (warten auf, denken an, sich freuen auf, träumen von) never change their preposition. Ask about them with wo(r)- for things and Präposition + wen/wem for people.
Fixed-preposition verbs ki preposition badalti nahi. Cheezon ke baare mein poochhna ho to wo(r)- use karo, aur logon ke baare mein poochhna ho to preposition ke saath wen ya wem.
hätte for wanting a thing, wäre for wanting to be somewhere/a state, würde + Infinitiv for wanting to do an action. Formal Sie always takes würden/könnten/hätten.
Koi cheez chahiye to hätte gern, kahin hona ya kisi state mein hona ho to wäre gern, aur kuch karna ho to würde gern ke saath Infinitiv.
When the relative pronoun is the subject, use Nominativ (der/die/das/die). When it's the object, use Akkusativ — only the masculine changes: der → den.
der Film, den ich gesehen habe
Relative pronoun subject ho to Nominativ aata hai, aur object ho to Akkusativ. Sirf masculine badalta hai — der se den.

The one move: weil sends the verb to the end
weil → conjugated verb goes to the very end of its clause. Comma always before weil.

A weil-clause cannot stand on its own — it is a piece hanging off the main sentence. German marks that by parking the verb at the far end, so you can hear from the word order alone that this half is not a full sentence.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich hier arbeiten möchte.

A main clause (Hauptsatz) keeps its verb in position 2. The moment you add weil, that clause becomes a Nebensatz and its conjugated verb jumps to the very end. A comma always comes before weil.

Only the weil-part changes — the main clause is untouched. Picture the verb being pushed to the wall at the end of the weil-clause.

Hauptsatz vs. Nebensatz — side by side
The same idea, two word orders. In the Hauptsatz the verb is second; in the Nebensatz it is last.
In the Nebensatz nothing sits in “position 2” — the verb waits at the back. That is the single visual difference to remember.

Every adjective has three steps. The Positiv is the plain form (schnell). The Komparativ adds -er and pairs with als ("than"): schneller als der Bus. The Superlativ tops the list — either am schnellsten (after a verb) or der/die/das schnellste (before a noun). Most short adjectives also take an umlaut: groß → größer → am größten, alt → älter, jung → jünger. Four irregulars carry the load in real speech and are worth memorising cold: gut → besser → am besten, viel → mehr → am meisten, gern → lieber → am liebsten, hoch → höher → am höchsten.

One question decides it — is a noun coming?
The superlative has two shapes. After a verb (or standing alone) use am ...-sten. Directly before a noun use der/die/das ...-ste.

Many one-syllable adjectives take an umlaut in the Komparativ and Superlativ. The vowel a/o/u gains two dots.
Not all short adjectives do this — e.g. schön → schöner (no umlaut). Learn the umlaut ones as a small set: groß, alt, jung, lang, kurz, warm, kalt, stark, schwach, klug.

A few very common words don’t follow the pattern at all. These four appear constantly — learn them by heart.

Chaar irregular zaroor yaad karo: gut→besser→am besten, viel→mehr→am meisten, gern→lieber→am liebsten, hoch→höher→am höchsten. "am liebsten" = sabse pasand.
Berlin ist mehr groß als München.
German adds -er to the adjective; it does not use "mehr" (more) like English.
After a comparative, "than" is als, not wie.
gut is irregular: besser / der beste (never "gutste").
The am-form ends in -sten: am schnellsten.

Char galtiyan common hain. English ki tarah mehr lagane ki zaroorat nahi — seedha -er lagao: größer. “Than” ke liye als aata hai, wie nahi. gut irregular hai, isliye der beste sahi hai, gutste nahi. Aur am-form -sten par khatam hoti hai: am schnellsten.
in + Dativ; mein → meinem (recycled — Possessiv Dativ).
die schönste — der/die/das + -ste before a noun (this chapter).
mit + Dativ; mein → meiner (recycled — Possessiv Dativ).

German splits comparisons in two, and one small word tells them apart. When two things are different, use the Komparativ + als: Anna ist größer als Max. When two things are the same, use (genau)so + plain adjective + wie: Ich bin so groß wie du. Notice the equality form keeps the adjective in its base shape (groß, gut, schön — never größer). You can strengthen it with genauso ... wie or ebenso ... wie ("just as ... as"). The classic slip is crossing the wires — größer wie, so größer als. One checklist keeps you safe: different → als, same → wie.

The split: different → als, same → wie
Different → Komparativ + als. Same → so + plain adjective + wie.
different: Anna ist größer als Max.
same: Ich bin so groß wie du.
Pehle rishta dekho, phir shabd chuno: barabar → wie, alag → als. Aur barabar wale mein adjective simple rehta hai — "so größer wie" kabhi nahi.
Equality keeps the plain adjective and pairs with wie.
Never mix: no so … als, no größer wie.
Every comparison is one of two kinds. If the two things are different, use the Komparativ + als. If they are the same, use (genau)so + plain adjective + wie.

The frame is so … wie. Strengthen with genauso / ebenso; negate with nicht so … wie.
